# Ingredient price shocks 2023–2026: evidence notes

Retrieved 2026-09-28. Every figure below comes from a row in `evidence.csv`, where the URL and publication date are recorded. Each section has two parts. **Sources report** covers only what the pages say. **Inference / not established** covers my reading of those pages and the gaps in them.

Rows marked "read via summarising fetch tool" were read through an intermediate summariser, not as raw page text. Check exact wording and figures on the page before quoting them in print.

---

## Cocoa / chocolate
**Sources report**
- Cocoa went from about $2,300–2,500/t in 2021–22 to over $12,000/t in 2024 (IFT, Reuters). ConfectioneryNews gives a record of $10.75/kg on 31 Jan 2025.
- By May 2026, futures were about 70% below the late-2024 peak (Reuters, Axios). Axios puts US futures at $3,889 on 21 May 2026.
- ICCO says the 2024/25 season ended in a small surplus of 37,000 t. Production rose 8.5% and grindings fell 3.3%.
- Manufacturers responded by shrinking bars, adding fillers and using compound or cocoa-free products (ChoViva, NextCoa, Win-Win, Choruba). Hershey says it will return to its original recipes in 2027. Barry Callebaut says real chocolate is now sometimes cheaper than compound (Reuters, May 2026).
- Barry Callebaut's academy chef advised UK bakers to use compound chocolate in muffins and cookies (British Baker).
- **Restaurants and pastry:**
  - Canada's 100 Best (June 2025): molten chocolate cake has "all but" left pub and bistro menus. Top pastry chefs say they now use good chocolate more sparingly.
  - Copenhagen's Friis-Holm saw costs rise 20–25%. It was cushioned by buying direct from South America (DR, Dec 2024).
  - London's TOAD Bakery, Lyaness and Apricity have featured the cocoa-free Win-Win Choc (IFT, July 2026).
  - Barcelona's pastry guild says chocolate-figure monas keep growing. 2026 mona prices rose only about €0.75 despite higher costs (EFE; CatalunyaPress).
- **Menu data:** Tastewise says 56.75% of US restaurants offer chocolate and that "social conversations" fell 23.32%. It gives no time window, sample size or trend over time.

**Conflicts**
- The Canada's 100 Best article says "chocolate prices" rose about 400%. That figure describes cocoa beans, not chocolate. Friis-Holm's 20–25% cost rise is much smaller.
- Hershey told Axios its recipe reversal was "not driven by cocoa prices". Reuters frames the reversal as price-driven.

**Inference / not established**
- I found no sourced menu-count data showing that chocolate desserts actually fell on restaurant menus. The molten-cake claim is one journalist's observation, not a count.
- I found no chef interviews that name carob as a replacement. Carob appears only as an ingredient inside industrial analogs.
- Cheaper cocoa is reaching retail with about a 10-month lag (Reuters). So 2026–27 may bring more chocolate back onto menus, but that has not been observed yet.

## Pistachio / "Dubai chocolate"
**Sources report**
- Kernel prices rose from $7.65/lb to about $10.30/lb in the year to April 2025, per one trader, Giles Hacking of CG Hacking (FT). The Guardian, FoodNavigator and others repeat that same figure.
- The FT gives two causes together: demand from the Dubai-chocolate craze (a TikTok video from Dec 2023 with over 120 million views), and tight supply. The 2024 US crop was small and was sold mainly in-shell, which left few kernels. California supply fell 20%. Iran's exports to the UAE rose 40%.
- The 2025 California crop was a record, about 1.6bn lb. A heat wave in March 2026 cut the 2026 crop to an estimated 700–800m lb (The Packer). Wonderful Pistachios says prices will rise, and Kern County lost 56% of its expected crop (NY Post).
- Terrain Ag says Google searches for the trend peaked in March 2025, but pistachio demand stayed strong in lattes, cookies and ice cream.

**Conflicts**
- The price-rise figure rests on one trader quote that everyone repeats. I found no American Pistachio Growers or INC price series.
- The FT's own reporting shows supply problems ran alongside the demand spike. "Demand caused it" is only half the story.

**Inference / not established**
- Pistachio is the clearest case of a price rise led partly by social-media demand. Even so, I could not separate how much came from demand and how much from the crop.
- The Puratos "+72% online popularity" figure has no stated metric or denominator. Do not use it as data.
- I found no sourced restaurant menu counts for pistachio desserts.

## Matcha
**Sources report**
- The first Kyoto tencha auction in May 2025 averaged ¥8,235/kg, a record (Reuters citing the Global Japanese Tea Association).
- The first JA Zennoh Kyoto tender of 2026, on 13 May, averaged ¥14,127/kg. That is the highest in 10 years, with a high of ¥40,021 (Shokuhin Shimbun).
- Causes named: the Kyoto heatwave in 2024 cut yields, and social-media demand surged from autumn 2024. Wholesalers rationed stock; Tealife's founder says his customers' demand grew tenfold (Reuters).
- Finance Ministry data for fiscal 2025 show green tea exports at 13,125 t (+42%) worth ¥84.7bn (2.2 times the year before). Powdered tea was about 70% of volume. Japan's imports of green tea rose 82% (Jiji).
- **Café responses (US only):**
  - Breadbelly in San Francisco paused its matcha drinks.
  - Blue Willow raised prices about 20% while its costs roughly doubled.
  - Andytown's supplier raised prices 60%, and it is testing blends.
  - Forest Tea Bar is pushing hojicha and genmaicha instead (SF Chronicle).
  - Tastewise: matcha item prices up 14% in US foodservice (Fresh Cup).

**Conflicts**
- Reuters says the ¥8,235 result was "a 170% increase" year on year. Other sellers describe it as about 1.7 times the prior year, which is a 70% rise. The two phrasings are not the same.
- Kettl's 2025 figure of ¥14,541 (+169%) is a different series (first-flush, machine-harvested average) from the first-tender averages. Do not mix the two.
- The 2026 Shokuhin figure of about ¥14,127 is roughly 1.7 times 2025's ¥8,235. Kettl's "~¥23,000" for 2026 is labelled "illustrative".

**Inference / not established**
- Matcha is the strongest documented demand-driven case: rising exports, rationing and switching to substitutes all appear together.
- Weather was also a cause, so this is not demand alone.
- I found no sourced café responses in Copenhagen, Barcelona or London.

## Hazelnut
**Sources report**
- An April 2025 frost hit Turkey, which grows about 70% of the world's hazelnuts. Prices rose more than 35% from April, and Turkish futures went above 200 lira/kg (DW).
- Crop estimates range widely: TurkStat 520,000 t, INC/KIB about 601,000 t, industry 450,000–550,000 t, and a UK importer says down more than 40%.
- INC reports prices at historic highs, carry-over stock being held back, and Italy's crop hit by premature fruit drop. A UK importer says Italy's harvest roughly halved to about 60,000 t.
- Ferrero told DW it does not expect disruption.

**Inference / not established**
- This was a supply shock, not a demand one.
- I found no sourced reporting on pastry-kitchen or restaurant responses, such as less praline or gianduja. That is a gap.
- I also found no Turkish export price series for 2026.

## Olive oil
**Sources report**
- Two drought years cut Spain's crop to about 660,000 t in 2022/23 (COAG, via El Español).
- In Spain, olive oil hit about €10/litre, up almost 40% in a year (Sept 2023). Bars responded:
  - charging for a second single-dose portion of oil;
  - raising the price of toast with oil;
  - spraying oil onto the plancha instead of pouring it;
  - one bar owner admitted refilling branded bottles with cheaper oil (El Español).
- The UK retail price of own-label oil rose 34% to £7.68/litre by Sept 2024 (The Grocer).
- The IOC says world production rose 38% in 2024/25, with Spain at 1.419 Mt (+66%). By December 2025, Jaén EVOO producer prices were €433 per 100 kg (-11% year on year).

**Inference / not established**
- Olive oil is a completed spike-and-fall.
- The restaurant responses found are Spanish bars, not the serious restaurants the newsletter covers. There is no evidence of lasting menu change.

## Coffee
**Sources report**
- ICO composite prices peaked around 355 US cents/lb in Feb–Apr 2025 and again at 343.92 on 11 Nov 2025. They fell to about 305 in December 2025 and averaged 273.70 in March 2026.
- ICO causes: deficits in three of the four years from 2021/22 to 2024/25, and EU consumer stocks nearly halved. In 2025, arabica rose while robusta fell 16.7%.
- A Middle East shock pushed prices up in March 2026, despite forecasts of a record Brazil crop.
- UK cafés: Lavazza's Regent Street café's dine-in flat white went from £5.50 to £6.50. Grind says green coffee more than doubled since 2024 and it makes 18p profit per £4.10 cup (Guardian via AOL, July 2026).

**Inference / not established**
- Coffee was driven by supply, weather and tariffs, not new demand.
- Evidence of café responses is limited to price rises. I found no evidence of menu substitution. Whether matcha is taking share from coffee in cafés was not checked.

## Butter, eggs, beef
**Sources report**
- **Butter:** EU butter rose 19% on average from Oct 2023 to Oct 2024, with Germany up 40% (AP). Paris pastry chef Arnaud Delmontel refuses to use margarine and is absorbing the cost. UK wholesale butter was 35% lower year on year by November 2025 (AHDB).
- **Eggs:** In the US bird-flu shortage, Waffle House charged 50 cents extra per egg from Feb to Jun 2025 and Denny's also added a surcharge. Retail eggs were still up more than 40% year on year in May 2025 (NPR).
- **Beef, UK:** The GB deadweight steer price was £6.98/kg in May 2025, up 25% year to date (AHDB). A UK catering buyer (allmanhall) is pushing part-vegetable burgers.
- **Beef, US:** Steaks averaged $12.80/lb in May 2026 (+16%). The cattle herd is at a 75-year low. A K-State economist says rising consumer demand is also pushing prices up (Fortune).

**Inference / not established**
- Butter and eggs have come back down.
- Beef is still high. It is partly a demand story in the US (demand rising two years running).
- I found no documented restaurant menu shifts away from beef in the three cities.

## Vanilla and saffron
**Sources report**
- **Vanilla:** Madagascar's export price fell 81% to $47.1/kg in Q1 2024 and revenue fell 64% (Bloomberg). A $50–70/kg export window restricted exports, and the 2025 crop was expected to be abundant (Cook's).
- **Saffron:** a seller's blog says EU imports in Jan–Aug 2025 reached record spending (+42%) at a unit value in the mid-€600s per kg.

**Inference / not established**
- Vanilla is now cheap by 2018–19 standards. I found no source linking that to vanilla returning to menus.
- The saffron evidence is weak (a seller blog relaying Mundus Agri). It needs a Eurostat Comext check.

## Newly used because cheap or trendy: ube
**Sources report**
- The Philippines banned fresh ube exports (FT, 21 Sept 2026). Farm-gate prices have more than doubled.
- US menu prevalence more than tripled from 2021 to 2025 (Datassential; no denominator given).
- Starbucks and Costa launched ube drinks in 2026. The ban excludes frozen and processed ube, which is what most restaurants use.
- London's Kapihan café and UK Filipino bakery Panadera are bracing for higher prices. A BMI analyst suggests purple sweet potato as a substitute.

**Inference / not established**
- Ube is the next case of social-media demand pushing up a price.
- Cocoa-free "chocolate" and compound chocolate are the clearest examples of an ingredient used because another got expensive. The evidence covers industry and bakery use (and three London venues through Win-Win), not broad restaurant use.
- I found no sourced case of chefs adopting an ingredient simply because it had become cheap. Vanilla and olive oil are candidates but are unevidenced.

---

## Cross-cutting: what is NOT established
1. **Price → menu causation.** Nothing I found links an ingredient price to counted changes in menus. The restaurant evidence is anecdote from named venues. The only menu statistics (Tastewise, Datassential) have no denominators or time series.
2. **Demand-driven price rises.** Sources clearly name demand as a cause for matcha, pistachio and ube, and partly for US beef. In every case, weather or supply was a cause at the same time.
3. **Lead cities.** Copenhagen evidence is Friis-Holm plus a fastelavnsbolle price check that blames general inflation. Barcelona evidence is the monas pieces. London evidence is the Win-Win venues, Kapihan/Panadera and the flat-white prices. None of it is systematic. This is a gap MISE's own menu data could fill.
